title: Aldehydes
path: Structure and Properties of Alcohols, Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids and Amines

headings.title: Introduction to Aldehydes and the Carbonyl Group
headings.content: An aldehyde is an organic compound featuring a **carbonyl group** bonded to at least one hydrogen atom. This functional group consists of a carbon atom double-bonded to an oxygen atom (-CHO). Because the carbonyl carbon in an aldehyde sits at the very end of the carbon chain, it always carries that crucial terminal hydrogen atom. This structural placement distinguishes aldehydes from ketones, where the carbonyl carbon is flanked by two carbon chains. In organic chemistry and pharmaceutical foundations for midwifery, understanding this basic framework helps explain how these compounds behave in both laboratory settings and living systems.

headings.title: Nomenclature and Structural Characteristics
headings.content: Naming aldehydes follows IUPAC guidelines by replacing the suffix '-ane' of the parent alkane with **'-al'**. For example, a one-carbon aldehyde is methanal, commonly known as formaldehyde. Because the functional group is inherently terminal, it automatically receives position number one in any carbon chain, making number locants unnecessary for the principal functional group. The geometry around the carbonyl carbon is **trigonal planar**, with bond angles of approximately 120 degrees due to sp2 hybridization. This flat geometry leaves the carbon open to attack from nucleophiles from either above or below the plane.

headings.title: Physical Properties: Boiling Points and Solubility
headings.content: Aldehydes are polar molecules because oxygen is significantly more electronegative than carbon, pulling shared electrons toward itself. This dipole-dipole attraction means aldehydes have higher boiling points than nonpolar alkanes of similar molecular weight, though lower boiling points than corresponding alcohols since aldehydes cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds with themselves. Smaller aldehydes dissolve readily in water because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules through their carbonyl oxygen. As the carbon chain lengthens beyond four or five carbons, the hydrophobic hydrocarbon portion dominates, causing water solubility to drop sharply.

headings.title: Laboratory Methods for Synthesizing Aldehydes
headings.content: Preparing aldehydes typically involves the controlled **oxidation of primary alcohols**. Because aldehydes oxidize further into carboxylic acids very easily, chemists use specialized reagents like **Pyridinium Chlorochromate (PCC)** in anhydrous solvents to stop the reaction at the aldehyde stage, preventing runaway oxidation. Another common preparation method is the reduction of carboxylic acid derivatives or acyl chlorides, though controlling reaction conditions remains critical to avoid over-reduction down to primary alcohols.

headings.title: Reactivity of the Carbonyl Carbon
headings.content: The carbonyl carbon is electron-deficient because oxygen pulls electron density away from it. This makes the carbon highly susceptible to **nucleophilic addition reactions**. A nucleophile with a pair of electrons attacks the partial positive carbon, pushing pi electrons from the double bond onto the oxygen atom. Factors influencing how fast this attack happens include steric hindrance—smaller aldehydes react faster because bulky groups block the incoming nucleophile—and electronic effects, since electron-withdrawing groups make the carbonyl carbon even more positive and reactive.

headings.title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions
headings.content: Aldehydes occupy a middle oxidation state between primary alcohols and carboxylic acids. Because they possess a hydrogen atom directly attached to the carbonyl carbon, they undergo **oxidation** extremely easily, turning into carboxylic acids using agents like potassium permanganate or chromic acid. Conversely, treating aldehydes with **reducing agents** like sodium borohydride (NaBH4) or lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH4) adds hydride ions to the carbonyl carbon, reducing them back into primary alcohols.

headings.title: Key Identification Tests: Tollen's and Fehling's Reagents
headings.content: Because aldehydes oxidize so readily, laboratory tests exploit this property to distinguish them from ketones. **Tollens' reagent** contains an ammoniacal silver nitrate solution; when heated with an aldehyde, it reduces silver ions to metallic silver, coating the test tube in a shiny 'silver mirror'. **Fehling's solution** uses copper(II) ions in an alkaline tartrate complex; reaction with an aldehyde reduces blue Cu2+ ions into a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide. Ketones fail to react under these mild conditions because they lack the oxidizable C-H bond.

headings.title: Biological Significance and Common Pharmaceutical Applications
headings.content: Aldehydes appear frequently in biochemistry and medicine. Formaldehyde (methanal) in aqueous solution forms formalin, historically used as a tissue fixative and preservative in anatomy laboratories. **Glucose**, a fundamental biological energy source, exists primarily in a cyclic hemiacetal form but contains an open-chain aldehyde form that participates in metabolic pathways and blood sugar testing. Other complex aldehydes act as vital intermediates in hormone synthesis, visual pigments in the retina, and antimicrobial agents in pharmacology.
